name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
strategy: Concentrated long book of five wide-moat, high-ROIC, net-cash compounders - GOOGL, V, NVDA, TSM, META - rebalanced away from second-derivative AI-capex exposure toward cash-generative and nominal-spend-linked franchises, with a 16% cash buffer earning 4% against a Fed that is hiking into a 5% ten-year.
reassessment_note: My strategy of record was written for a 'no-rate-cut macro'. That is no longer the regime and I was wrong to keep sizing for it. As of the 2026-09-15 tape the 10-year Treasury is at 5.01%, its highest since 2007; futures price a 92.5% probability of a rate HIKE at tomorrow's FOMC, with a new Chair explicitly looking to establish credibility; August core CPI posted its largest four-month increase; Brent is $106 on Middle East supply risk. That is a rising-discount-rate, cost-push regime, and it is the single biggest change in my thinking. The quality screen itself survives it - wide-moat, high-ROIC, genuinely net-cash businesses are precisely what you want when the risk-free rate rises, because they do not need to refinance and their value is not all in the terminal year. What does not survive it is WHICH quality names I owned. Second shock: Amodei, Altman and xAI's leadership publicly called for slowing the pace of AI capability development. Supply-chain checks (Lynx) find zero actual GPU slowdown - no cancellations at TSMC or OSATs, no schedule changes at semicap - so I read the move as a sentiment derating rather than demand destruction. But the derating lands hardest on companies selling FUTURE fab capacity, and with the discount rate rising a sentiment derating has room to run. So I am cutting the second-derivative leg entirely and reducing, not eliminating, the first-derivative legs. Three specific changes. (1) AMAT exits at 0% from 14%. Its business is fine - record $9.12bn quarter, +25%, positive Q4 guide - but it is down 27.6% over 63 days and 16.3% over 21, and my edge is not in forecasting whether hyperscaler capex converts to tool orders on schedule. The mandate is to buy quality at 19-26x after a pullback, not to average down into an open capex-cycle question the day the Fed hikes. (2) NVDA and TSM are trimmed from 24% each to 15% each, cutting AI-supplier exposure from 62% of the book to 30%. (3) I add V at 16% and META at 14% - both wide-moat, high-ROIC compounders whose revenue is linked to nominal spending rather than to fab capex, which is the correct exposure when inflation is the thing running hot. GOOGL is trimmed only to fund, from 26% to 24%, and remains the largest position. One timing point that shapes the sizing: my fill is the 2026-09-16 close, which is AFTER the decision and the guidance print. I am therefore not paying for event gap risk, and I have not over-cashed for it. The 16% cash is not a hedge against tomorrow; it is compensation for the fact that a 5% ten-year is a multi-month multiple problem for everything I own, and at 4% APY cash is for the first time a genuinely competitive asset in this book.

positions.thesis: Largest position and the best regime fit in the book. Alphabet is an AI USER, not an AI-capex supplier, so the pacing call that just repriced the semis complex is neutral-to-positive for it: if hyperscaler buildout paces, Google's depreciation burden eases and free cash flow improves, while Search keeps earning enormous cash TODAY rather than in a terminal year that a 5% discount rate punishes. It is the only leg of the outgoing book in the green (+2.13%), it is still 15% below its 52-week high, and it carries roughly $95bn of net cash so a hiking Fed costs it nothing on the liability side. Cloud is compounding on real enterprise wins (Salesforce partnership expansion, new Singapore engineering centre this week). Trimmed two points only to fund the new legs, not on any change of view. The 18% stop is wider than the name's realised volatility because I want it to survive a macro drawdown, not a macro wobble.

New position, and the single most deliberate addition. Visa is the cleanest quality compounder for THIS macro: a duopoly payments network with 30%+ ROIC, near-zero incremental capital intensity and a moat that is regulatory and behavioural rather than technological. Critically, its revenue is a toll on nominal consumer spending - so $106 Brent and accelerating core CPI mechanically raise its top line, which makes it one of the very few genuine inflation beneficiaries that still clears a quality-compounder screen. It has no exposure whatsoever to fab capex, hyperscaler order books or the AI pacing debate, which is exactly the diversification this book was missing when 62% of it sat in one supply chain. At ~25x forward it is not cheap, but it has compounded 15.7% over 63 days while the semis complex fell, and paying a fair multiple for earnings that inflate with the price level beats paying a low multiple for earnings levered to a capex cycle in question. Sized at 16% - large enough to matter, below the semis legs it partly replaces. Tighter 14% stop than the rest because this is a lower-beta name and a 14% drawdown here would mean my regime read was simply wrong.

Kept but cut from 24% to 15%. The quality case is intact and is the strongest in the market: extreme ROIC, large net cash, and independent supply-chain checks this week found no GPU rollout slowdown, no memory or flash cancellations and no delivery schedule changes anywhere in the ecosystem - the Amodei essay explicitly did not call for slowing hardware rollout, and Anthropic has a direct financial incentive for compute to keep expanding. So I do not believe the demand story broke. What did change is that NVDA is the market's AI beta expression, and in a week where the real drivers are a 5% long bond and geopolitical risk, beta is a liability I do not want at 24%. Down 5.4% in five sessions and 5.2% in 21 with the leg 5.23% underwater, it is already absorbing the derating. Halving toward 15% keeps the upside if the selloff is the sentiment overshoot the order books suggest, while ending the situation where one narrative could move a quarter of my book. The 35% take-profit exists precisely because a sentiment-driven derating with intact fundamentals is the setup that snaps back hardest.

Kept but cut from 24% to 15% for the same portfolio-construction reason as NVDA. On the merits TSMC is the highest-quality asset in the entire semiconductor chain: an effective leading-edge foundry monopoly with pricing power over its own customers, substantial net cash, and revenue diversified across smartphone, AI, auto and industrial rather than levered to any one buyer - MediaTek's newest smartphone parts on its latest node this week are a reminder that the non-AI half of the business is real. It fell 3.3% on a 2028 roadmap and High-NA adoption story, which is a story about capital intensity years out, not about current demand; supply-chain checks found no cancellations at TSMC. That makes it the leg I am most comfortable still owning after the shock. But it is a Taiwan-domiciled asset in a week when the honest analyst read is that geopolitics and US-China export controls, not AI demand, are driving semis weakness, and that risk is not one I can underwrite. 15% respects the quality and respects the tail. Wide 20% stop because a geopolitical gap would not be a thesis error I could trade around.

New position. Meta clears the mandate screen cleanly - wide moat in the form of four billion-user network effects, ROIC among the highest in mega-cap, net cash, and a management team that has demonstrated it will cut costs hard when the market demands it. Two things make it the right addition now rather than a generic quality name. First, like Alphabet it is an AI spender rather than an AI supplier, so a genuine pacing of the buildout converts directly into lower depreciation and higher free cash flow - it is on the correct side of the shock that just hit my book. Second, advertising revenue is nominal-GDP-linked, so like Visa it does not shrink in real terms when inflation runs hot. It has outperformed sharply into this weakness, +9.3% over five sessions and +13.7% over 21 while the semis complex fell, which tells me the rotation out of AI-capex beta and into AI-monetisation cash flows is already underway and I am joining it rather than calling it. Still roughly 15% below its 52-week high, and of 55 covering analysts none rates it sell. Sized at 14%, the smallest equity leg, because the multiple is the least discounted part of the case and its own capex line is the one thing that could disappoint.
